title: Job 41 — Leviathan, king over all the proud

paragraphs.text: הֵן־תֹּחַלְתּ֥וֹ נִכְזָ֑בָה הֲגַ֖ם אֶל־מַרְאָ֣יו יֻטָֽל׃

i18n.en: Behold, the hope of him is disappointed — even at the sight of him is one cast down?

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter opens on capture-disappointment.** *Tochalto nikhzavah* — *the hope of him is disappointed*. Anyone who hoped to subdue Leviathan finds his expectation thwarted. *Ha-gam el-mar'av yutal* — *is one even at the sight of him cast down*? The mere visual presence of Leviathan is overwhelming. // The verse continues the unsubdueability argument from chapter 40. The English chapter division (where this verse is Job 41:9) breaks the continuity that the Hebrew preserves — the Leviathan description flows from 40:25 to 41:26 in the Hebrew without chapter-boundary, but the English tradition splits 41:1 at what is 40:25 in Hebrew and starts 41:9 (English) here at Hebrew 41:1.

paragraphs.text: לֹֽא־אַ֭כְזָר כִּ֣י יְעוּרֶ֑נּוּ וּמִ֥י ה֝֗וּא לְפָנַ֥י יִתְיַצָּֽב׃

i18n.en: None is so fierce that they would dare rouse him — and who is he that can stand before me?

paragraphs.commentary: **The pivot from Leviathan to YHWH.** The verse turns on a remarkable rhetorical structure: *no one is fierce enough to rouse Leviathan* ... *and who can stand before me*? The chapter is making an **a-fortiori argument**: if no one can take on Leviathan, certainly no one can take on Leviathan's *maker*. The chapter has staged Leviathan as the most-fearsome accessible creature — and uses that fear-status to magnify YHWH's status. // The verb *yityatzav* (stand before, present oneself before) is the same form as in Job 1:6, 2:1 (the bnei ha-elohim *presenting themselves* before YHWH; see [`mit'yatzev-al-YHWH`](/wiki/mit-yatzev-al-YHWH/)). The chapter is invoking the council-presentation register — but now in inverted form: who could *stand* before YHWH in the adversarial-litigation sense Job has been attempting?

paragraphs.text: מִ֣י הִ֭קְדִּימַנִי וַאֲשַׁלֵּ֑ם תַּ֖חַת כָּל־הַשָּׁמַ֣יִם לִי־הֽוּא׃

i18n.en: Who has come before me, that I should repay? Under all the skies, it is mine.

paragraphs.commentary: **The ownership-claim.** *Tachat kol ha-shamayim li-hu* — *under all the skies, it is mine*. The chapter is staking the **comprehensive cosmic ownership claim**: everything under the heavens belongs to YHWH. The verse interrupts the Leviathan description with this brief assertion before returning to the description.

paragraphs.text: לא־[לֽוֹ־] אַחֲרִ֥ישׁ בַּדָּ֑יו וּדְבַר־גְּ֝בוּר֗וֹת וְחִ֣ין עֶרְכּֽוֹ׃

i18n.en: I will not keep silent about his limbs, or his mighty deeds, or the grace of his proportion.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter announces its descriptive mission.** *Lo achrish badav* — *I will not keep silent about his limbs*. The chapter is going to **describe Leviathan in detail** — limbs, deeds, proportions. The next 22 verses (vv 5-26) are sustained physical description. // *Ketiv/qere* note: *lo* (qere) for *l'* (ketiv) — the difference is *to him* (ketiv) vs. *not* (qere). The qere is the standard reading: 'I will not keep silent'.

paragraphs.text: מִֽי־גִ֭לָּה פְּנֵ֣י לְבוּשׁ֑וֹ בְּכֶ֥פֶל רִ֝סְנ֗וֹ מִ֣י יָבֽוֹא׃

i18n.en: Who has unveiled the face of his garment? Into the double of his bridle, who shall come?

paragraphs.commentary: **Leviathan's outer covering.** *Penei l'vusho* — *the face of his garment*. Leviathan has a *l'vush* — a *garment, outer covering* — and a *resen* — a *bridle, double-layer mouth-restraint*. The chapter is describing his outer surface as a **layered defensive armor**, with the next verses (vv 6-9) detailing the scale-system.

paragraphs.text: דַּלְתֵ֣י פָ֭נָיו מִ֣י פִתֵּ֑חַ סְבִיב֖וֹת שִׁנָּ֣יו אֵימָֽה׃

i18n.en: Who can open the doors of his face? Around his teeth is terror.

paragraphs.commentary: **Doors-of-his-face and teeth-of-terror.** *Daltei panav* — *doors of his face* — names the jaws as **closable doors**. The architectural-mechanical register (*daltayim* — doors) recurs from Job 38:8-10 (the sea-restraint doors). The same vocabulary describes Leviathan's anatomy: his jaws are *gates*. // *Aimah* — *terror, dread* — surrounds his teeth. The terror is not just an effect on observers but is **circumambient** to the teeth themselves — a property of the creature, not just a response in the observer.

paragraphs.text: גַּ֭אֲוָה אֲפִיקֵ֣י מָֽגִנִּ֑ים סָ֝ג֗וּר חוֹתָ֥ם צָֽר׃

i18n.en: His pride is the channels of shields, shut up as with a tight seal.

paragraphs.commentary: **The shield-scales.** *Afiqei maginnim* — *channels of shields*. The chapter is naming Leviathan's scales as **rows of shields**: armor-plates arranged in channels along his body. *Sagur chotam tzar* — *shut up as with a tight seal*. The seal-metaphor names the **interlocking tightness** of the scale-plate system. // The image is consistent with the heavy armor-scales of crocodilians (the standard scholarly identification for Leviathan is the Nile crocodile). Each scale is heavy keratinous bone-backed plate; the arrangement in rows along the back creates an interlocking armored surface. The Hebrew vocabulary (*shield*, *seal*) is precise to this anatomy.

paragraphs.text: אֶחָ֣ד בְּאֶחָ֣ד יִגַּ֑שׁוּ וְ֝ר֗וּחַ לֹא־יָב֥וֹא בֵֽינֵיהֶֽם׃

i18n.en: One to another they touch — and no breath comes between them.

paragraphs.commentary: **The scale-tightness specified.** *Echad b-echad yiggashu* — *one to one they touch*. *V-ruach lo yavo beneihem* — *and no breath comes between them*. // The chapter is naming the **air-tight** interlocking of the scale-armor: not even *ruach* (wind, breath) penetrates between the scales. The image is precision-engineered armor. The verbal echo of *ruach* (the same noun as in ch 1:2's *ruach Elohim*, in the chayyot's *ruach-chayyah*, and throughout Job) is part of the lens-relevant vocabulary cluster. Leviathan's armor is impenetrable even to the *ruach*.

paragraphs.text: אִישׁ־בְּאָחִ֥יהוּ יְדֻבָּ֑קוּ יִ֝תְלַכְּד֗וּ וְלֹ֣א יִתְפָּרָֽדוּ׃

i18n.en: Each cleaves to its brother — they are joined and cannot be separated.

paragraphs.commentary: **The scale-fusion.** *Ish b-achihu y'dubaqu* — *each cleaves to its brother*. *Yitlakkadu v-lo yitparadu* — *they are joined and cannot be separated*. The chapter completes the scale-armor description: the scales are fused, locked together, inseparable. The armor-system is **single-piece** in operation, multi-scale in structure.

paragraphs.text: עֲ‍ֽ֭טִישֹׁתָיו תָּ֣הֶל א֑וֹר וְ֝עֵינָ֗יו כְּעַפְעַפֵּי־שָֽׁחַר׃

i18n.en: His sneezes flash light, and his eyes are like the eyelids of dawn.

paragraphs.commentary: **Light-emitting sneezes.** *Atishotav tahel or* — *his sneezes flash light*. The chapter is naming Leviathan as a creature whose **sneezes emit light** — a phenomenon the chapter does not explain but names directly. // The image has been read in multiple ways: (1) **sun-reflection** — sneeze-spray catches sunlight at certain angles, producing rainbow / refraction effects (the standard naturalistic reading for the crocodile identification); (2) **bioluminescence-like phenomenon** — some kind of inherent light-emission (lens-relevant; matches the dragon-tradition's fire-breathing imagery in adjacent verses); (3) **mythological-cosmological** (Leviathan as the cosmic-sea creature whose body-functions are themselves cosmic-phenomena). // *Einav k-af'apei shachar* — *his eyes are like the eyelids of dawn*. The same image is reused in Egyptian hieroglyphics for the crocodile-eye motif (the *Heru-eye* / *Sun-eye* connection). The chapter is invoking iconographic-symbolic eye-imagery — the dawn-eye signifying first-light, watchful presence. The Babylonian Talmud (b. Berakhot 3a) takes this verse as the etymological source of the morning-eye motif in Jewish liturgy.

paragraphs.text: מִ֭פִּיו לַפִּידִ֣ים יַהֲלֹ֑כוּ כִּיד֥וֹדֵי אֵ֝֗שׁ יִתְמַלָּֽטוּ׃

i18n.en: From his mouth go forth torches; sparks of fire shoot out.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Mipiv lappidim yahalokhu*** — *from his mouth go forth torches*. *Kidodei esh yitmalatu* — *sparks of fire shoot out*. // This is the chapter's most-iconic Leviathan image: **fire from the mouth**. The vocabulary is precise: *lappidim* (torches — burning brands of fire) and *kidodei esh* (sparks of fire — embers, glowing fragments). The chapter is describing Leviathan as a **fire-breathing creature**. // The image is direct: Leviathan emits fire from his mouth. The standard scholarly readings have proposed: (1) **mythological-poetic** (the canonical Hebrew Bible dragon-tradition image, paralleled in Ugaritic, Mesopotamian, and broader ANE dragon-iconography); (2) **crocodilian breath-misting** (in cold morning air, the crocodile's warm breath produces visible vapor that looks like smoke/fire — but the *lappidim* / *kidodei esh* vocabulary is stronger than just vapor); (3) **literal fire-emission** (the chapter's plain reading; no known biological mechanism matches but the chapter's account is unambiguous). // The Wheel of Heaven lens reads this passage in continuity with: Genesis 1:21's *tanninim* (great dragons, taninim glossary entry, v2.0.0); Isaiah 27:1's identification of Leviathan with the *tannin* in the sea; the global dragon-tradition's fire-breathing motif (European dragons, Mesopotamian Tiamat, Chinese *long*); and the canonical fire-from-mouth imagery in apocalyptic-cosmic-battle texts (Rev 11:5, Rev 12 of the dragon). The chapter is staging Leviathan as the canonical **fire-breathing sea-dragon** of the Hebrew Bible's cosmic-creature vocabulary.

paragraphs.text: מִ֭נְּחִירָיו יֵצֵ֣א עָשָׁ֑ן כְּד֖וּד נָפ֣וּחַ וְאַגְמֹֽן׃

i18n.en: From his nostrils smoke goes out, like a boiling pot blown on, and the rush.

paragraphs.commentary: **Smoke from nostrils.** *Mi-n'chirav yetze ashan* — *from his nostrils smoke goes out*. The fire-mouth (v 11) and the smoke-nostrils (v 12) together complete the canonical **dragon-fire-and-smoke** imagery. // *K-dud nafuach v-agmon* — *like a boiling pot blown on, and the rush*. The boiling-pot imagery names the **roaring-vapor** quality of the smoke emission. The reading is mechanical-thermal: Leviathan's internal heat is so intense that smoke pours from his nostrils as from a kettle being blown to flame.

paragraphs.text: נַ֭פְשׁוֹ גֶּחָלִ֣ים תְּלַהֵ֑ט וְ֝לַ֗הַב מִפִּ֥יו יֵצֵֽא׃

i18n.en: His breath kindles coals, and flame goes out of his mouth.

paragraphs.commentary: **The fire-source is the *nefesh*.** *Nafsho gechalim t'lahet* — *his breath kindles coals*. The chapter is locating the fire-source in Leviathan's *nefesh* (breath, life-soul) — the same word as in Gen 2:7 (the human becomes a *nefesh chayyah* — *living being*). // The verse is the chapter's clearest statement of Leviathan's **fire-emission mechanism**: his *nefesh* itself burns; coals catch fire from his breath; flame issues from his mouth. The phenomenon is internal to the creature, not external (he doesn't have to be lit; he is on fire from within).

paragraphs.text: בְּֽ֭צַוָּארוֹ יָלִ֣ין עֹ֑ז וּ֝לְפָנָ֗יו תָּד֥וּץ דְּאָבָֽה׃

i18n.en: In his neck dwells strength, and dismay leaps before his face.

paragraphs.text: מַפְּלֵ֣י בְשָׂר֣וֹ דָבֵ֑קוּ יָצ֥וּק עָ֝לָ֗יו בַּל־יִמּֽוֹט׃

i18n.en: The folds of his flesh cleave together — cast firm upon him, they do not move.

paragraphs.text: לִ֭בּוֹ יָצ֣וּק כְּמוֹ־אָ֑בֶן וְ֝יָצ֗וּק כְּפֶ֣לַח תַּחְתִּֽית׃

i18n.en: His heart is cast firm as stone — yes, cast firm as a millstone's lower part.

paragraphs.text: מִ֭שֵּׂתוֹ יָג֣וּרוּ אֵלִ֑ים מִ֝שְּׁבָרִ֗ים יִתְחַטָּֽאוּ׃

i18n.en: At his rising, mighty ones fear; at the crashings, they purify themselves.

paragraphs.commentary: **The mighty ones fear.** *Yaguru elim* — *mighty ones fear*. *Elim* is plural of *el* — *mighty ones, divine beings*. The word is the same root as *Elohim*, *El Shaddai*, *Elohei Yisrael*. The chapter is naming **even divine-class beings** as *fearing* at Leviathan's rising. // The lens reads this with attention: Leviathan is fearsome **even to the divine-class beings** (the *elim*, possibly the same class as the *bnei ha-elohim* of 1:6, 2:1, 38:7). The chapter is positioning Leviathan as a creature that **gives pause to the council itself**. The combined fire-and-cosmic-fear register is consistent with the apocalyptic-dragon tradition (Rev 12:7-9 the dragon making war with the angels).

paragraphs.text: מַשִּׂיגֵ֣הוּ חֶ֭רֶב בְּלִ֣י תָק֑וּם חֲנִ֖ית מַסָּ֣ע וְשִׁרְיָֽה׃

i18n.en: If one attacks him with the sword, it will not stand — nor the spear, the dart, or the breastplate.

paragraphs.commentary: **Weapon-resistance catalog.** *Cherev* (sword), *chanit* (spear), *massa* (dart, javelin), *shiryah* (breastplate / shirt-of-mail). The chapter is naming the **standard military armaments** as ineffective against Leviathan. None of these weapons stand against him.

paragraphs.text: יַחְשֹׁ֣ב לְתֶ֣בֶן בַּרְזֶ֑ל לְעֵ֖ץ רִקָּב֣וֹן נְחוּשָֽׁה׃

i18n.en: He counts iron as straw, bronze as rotten wood.

paragraphs.commentary: **Metallurgical-strength inversion.** *Barzel* (iron) is counted as *teven* (straw). *Nechushah* (bronze) is counted as *etz riqavon* (rotten wood). The chapter is inverting the canonical Hebrew Bible **metal-strength hierarchy**: what humans consider hardest (iron) is *straw* to Leviathan; what humans consider firm (bronze) is *rotten wood*. // The verse establishes Leviathan as a creature whose **physical strength exceeds the entire human metallurgical-weapons-armor system**. The same iron-and-bronze that Behemoth had **for bones** (40:18 — *bones as bronze channels, limbs as iron bars*) is what Leviathan **counts as nothing**. The two creatures together are positioned as **beyond the human metallurgical-civilization frame**.

paragraphs.text: לֹֽא־יַבְרִיחֶ֥נּוּ בֶן־קָ֑שֶׁת לְ֝קַ֗שׁ נֶהְפְּכוּ־ל֥וֹ אַבְנֵי־קָֽלַע׃

i18n.en: The arrow does not make him flee; sling-stones are turned to chaff for him.

paragraphs.text: כְּ֭קַשׁ נֶחְשְׁב֣וּ תוֹתָ֑ח וְ֝יִשְׂחַ֗ק לְרַ֣עַשׁ כִּידֽוֹן׃

i18n.en: Clubs are counted as chaff — he laughs at the rattling of the javelin.

paragraphs.text: תַּ֭חְתָּיו חַדּ֣וּדֵי חָ֑רֶשׂ יִרְפַּ֖ד חָר֣וּץ עֲלֵי־טִֽיט׃

i18n.en: Underneath him are sharp potsherds; he spreads as a threshing-sledge upon the mud.

paragraphs.text: יַרְתִּ֣יחַ כַּסִּ֣יר מְצוּלָ֑ה יָ֝֗ם יָשִׂ֥ים כַּמֶּרְקָחָֽה׃

i18n.en: He makes the deep boil like a pot; he stirs the sea like a perfumer's mixing-bowl.

paragraphs.commentary: **Leviathan agitates the deep.** *Yartiach ka-sir m'tzulah* — *he makes the deep boil like a pot*. *Yam yasim ka-mirqachah* — *he stirs the sea like a perfumer's mixing-bowl*. // *M'tzulah* (depth, abyss) and *yam* (sea) name the **deep-water domain** as Leviathan's habitat. He stirs the sea **like a pot being boiled** — a thermal-mechanical image. The chapter is staging Leviathan as a creature whose movements **affect the deep-water domain on cosmic scale** — when Leviathan moves, the sea itself boils.

paragraphs.text: אַ֭חֲרָיו יָאִ֣יר נָתִ֑יב יַחְשֹׁ֖ב תְּה֣וֹם לְשֵׂיבָֽה׃

i18n.en: He leaves a shining path behind him — one would think the deep had grey hair.

paragraphs.commentary: **The wake.** *Acharav ya'ir nativ* — *behind him a path shines*. The verb *ya'ir* — *gives light, makes shine* — names the **luminous wake** Leviathan leaves as he moves through the deep. // *Yachshov tehom l-seyvah* — *one would think the deep had grey hair*. *Seyvah* (grey hair, white hair, age-whiteness) is used as a metaphor for the **white-foaming wake** behind the moving creature: the deep looks aged, white-haired, in Leviathan's wake. // The verb *yachshov* (think, reckon, compute) is poetic-attributive: *one would calculate / reckon* the deep to have grey hair. The chapter is using a **bioluminescence-or-foam** image for the visible wake. The reading is striking — Leviathan leaves a **luminous trail** through the deep. // *Tehom* is the same primordial-deep word as Gen 1:2 (see [`tehom`](/wiki/tehom/)). The chapter's *tehom* is Leviathan's territory.

paragraphs.text: אֵֽין־עַל־עָפָ֥ר מָשְׁל֑וֹ הֶ֝עָשׂ֗וּ לִבְלִי־חָֽת׃

i18n.en: There is no rule of him upon the dust — he was made without fear.

paragraphs.commentary: **No earthly counterpart.** *Ein al-afar mosh'lo* — *there is no rule of him upon the dust*. *Afar* (dust) is the Hebrew Bible's standard term for the **terrestrial human-creaturely domain** (Gen 2:7 — humanity formed *from the dust of the ground*). The chapter is asserting that on the *terrestrial dust-domain*, there is nothing like Leviathan, nothing that *rules* in his manner. // *He'asu li-vli chat* — *he was made without fear*. The chapter names Leviathan as the canonical **fearless creature** — created without the capacity for fear that all earthly creatures (including humans) have. The verse closes the description with the singular-class affirmation: Leviathan is **without equal among created beings**.

paragraphs.text: אֵֽת־כָּל־גָּבֹ֥הַּ יִרְאֶ֑ה ה֝֗וּא מֶ֣לֶךְ עַל־כָּל־בְּנֵי־שָֽׁחַץ׃ (ס)

i18n.en: He sees everything that is high; he is king over all the sons of pride.

paragraphs.commentary: **The closing identification: King over all the sons of pride.** ***Hu melekh al kol bnei shachatz*** — *he is king over all the sons of pride*. // *Bnei shachatz* — *sons of pride* — is a hapax-style compound (occurring only here in this specific form). *Shachatz* (שָׁחַץ) is rare; the same noun appears at Job 28:8 (*bnei shachatz* — *sons of the proud*, parallel to wild beasts). The compound names a class of **proud / lofty / wild** creatures. // The chapter closes Leviathan's description by **declaring him king** of the class. The structural-rhetorical close is significant: the chapter's second divine speech opened (40:9-14) with a challenge for Job to *humble all that is proud* (*ge'eh*, *gei'im*). Now the chapter closes with **Leviathan as king over all proud creatures** — the exact category Job was challenged to subdue. The frame is closed: Job cannot subdue the pride-class because Leviathan, who is king of that class, is unsubdueable by Job. // The structural connection from 40:11-13 (the challenge to humble the proud) to 41:26 (Leviathan as king of the proud) is the chapter's keystone argument: **humbling the proud is divine work, not human work** — because the king of the proud is a creature only the creator can subdue. The chapter has staged Leviathan as the **proof-by-example** of the impossibility of human-cosmic-justice-administration. // The divine speeches are now structurally complete. Chapter 42 will record Job's full response (vv 1-6) and the restoration epilogue (vv 7-17).
